related_questions.snippet: Nearly 1.2 million people in the United States are living with HIV, and approximately 13% of them don't know it. Estimated new HIV acquisitions decreased 12% from 36,300 in 2018 to 31,800 in 2022, propelled by a 30% decrease among young people aged 13-24 years.

related_questions.question: How long can a person live with HIV?

text_blocks.snippet: With effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV can live a normal lifespan and enjoy a good quality of life. Untreated, HIV progresses to AIDS, which is inevitably fatal, but ART can prevent this progression. The impact of HIV on lifespan depends on factors like early diagnosis, adherence to treatment, and overall health.
snippet_highlighted_words: With effective antiretroviral therapy (ART), people with HIV can live a normal lifespan

list.title: Early Diagnosis and Treatment:
list.snippet: Starting ART soon after diagnosis is crucial for maintaining a healthy immune system and preventing the progression to AIDS.

list.title: ART Adherence:
list.snippet: Consistent and proper use of ART is essential for keeping the virus suppressed and the immune system healthy.

list.title: Overall Health and Lifestyle:
list.snippet: Factors like smoking, drug use, and other health conditions can impact life expectancy for people with HIV, just as they do for those without HIV.

list.title: Access to Care:
list.snippet: Consistent access to quality medical care and monitoring is vital for managing HIV and optimizing treatment outcomes.

list.title: CD4 Count:
list.snippet: Higher CD4 counts (a type of white blood cell) indicate a stronger immune system. Lower CD4 counts can signify that HIV is progressing and treatment may need to be adjusted.

list.title: Viral Load:
list.snippet: A low or undetectable viral load (the amount of HIV in the blood) achieved through ART indicates that the virus is suppressed, which is important for both individual health and preventing transmission.

list.title: Early Stage:
list.snippet: HIV can be asymptomatic for many years, during which time the virus is still active and replicating.

list.title: AIDS:
list.snippet: If left untreated, HIV can progress to AIDS, characterized by a severely damaged immune system and increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: With effective ART, many individuals with HIV can live long, healthy lives, and some may never progress to AIDS.

list.title: Without treatment:
list.snippet: Without ART, the median survival time from HIV seroconversion (when the body first develops antibodies to HIV) was 8 to 10 years, according to The Lancet.

list.title: AIDS diagnosis:
list.snippet: With an AIDS diagnosis, individuals typically lived for about three years without treatment.

list.title: Life expectancy:
list.snippet: Thanks to advancements in ART, life expectancy for people with HIV can be similar to that of the general population, especially with early diagnosis and consistent treatment.

list.title: Impact of ART:
list.snippet: In the past, ART regimens had significant side effects, but modern combinations are generally well-tolerated and easier to manage.

text_blocks.snippet: Key takeaway: While HIV is a serious condition, it is now a manageable chronic disease with the right treatment and care. People with HIV can live long, healthy lives and protect others by maintaining an undetectable viral load.

African Americans have the highest percentage of HIV diagnoses in the South, Northeast, and Midwest, and Hispanics/ Latinos have the highest percentage in the West. text_blocks.snippet: In the United States, HIV/AIDS remains a significant public health issue, with over 1.2 million people living with HIV and an estimated 31,800 new infections in 2022. While new infections have decreased, progress has slowed, and disparities persist among certain populations.
snippet_highlighted_words: over 1.2 million people living with HIV and an estimated 31,800 new infections in 2022

list.snippet: Prevalence: Over 1.2 million people in the US are living with HIV.
New Infections: In 2022, there were an estimated 31,800 new HIV infections.
Disparities: Racial and ethnic minorities, particularly Black/African American and Hispanic/Latino individuals, experience a disproportionate burden of HIV.
Geographic Distribution: The South has the highest number of new HIV diagnoses.
Undiagnosed: Approximately 13% of people with HIV are unaware of their status.
Mortality: Around 8,000 people die each year with HIV-related illness as a contributing cause of death.

list.title: Public Health Threat:
list.snippet: HIV/AIDS continues to be a major public health concern, impacting individuals, families, and communities.

list.title: Economic Burden:
list.snippet: The US government spends approximately $20 billion annually on direct health expenditures for HIV prevention and care.

list.title: Social and Structural Factors:
list.snippet: HIV stigma, homophobia, discrimination, poverty, and limited access to healthcare contribute to inequities in HIV outcomes.

list.title: Decline in Infections:
list.snippet: Estimated new HIV infections decreased by 12% between 2018 and 2022.

list.title: Focus on Prevention:
list.snippet: The US government is working to end the HIV epidemic through various strategies, including prevention, testing, and treatment.

list.title: Treatment Advancements:
list.snippet: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has transformed HIV from a fatal illness to a manageable chronic condition.

list.title: Undetectable=Untransmittable:
list.snippet: People with HIV who are on effective ART and have an undetectable viral load cannot transmit the virus to others.

list.title: Continued Prevention Efforts:
list.snippet: Increased access to testing, prevention, and treatment services is crucial to further reduce new infections.

list.title: Addressing Disparities:
list.snippet: Targeted interventions and resources are needed to address the disproportionate impact of HIV on specific communities.

list.title: Eliminating Stigma:
list.snippet: Reducing stigma and discrimination related to HIV is essential to ensure that everyone has access to the care and support they need.

list.title: Sustaining Progress:
list.snippet: Continued investment and commitment are needed to maintain and accelerate progress in the fight against HIV/AIDS in the US.
